newsitem.title: USA: CIA shipped arms to Guatemala guerrillas - report.
newsitem.headline: CIA shipped arms to Guatemala guerrillas - report.

text.p: The CIA secretly shipped a planeload of weapons to leftist rebels in Guatemala in 1982, while the United States was trying to forge an anti-communist alliance in Central America, a newspaper reported on Sunday.

The CIA hoped the arms shipment to guerrillas backed by Cuban President Fidel Castro would pay dividends in Nicaragua, where the agency was assembling groups of anti-communist insurgents into the contra army, the Miami Herald reported.

The CIA was trying to lure a former Nicaragua Sandinista commander to change sides and join the contras. He demanded weapons for his friends in Guatemala as a sign of the agency's sincerity, the Herald said.
The newspaper said the agency's role in the weapons shipment came to light last week in a series of interviews.

The arms shipment was a closely held secret from U.S. allies in Guatemala City and from most U.S. officials working on Central America policy. The weapons were delivered during a guerrilla offensive that some Guatemalan military officials said nearly toppled the government, the Herald reported.
Roger Fontaine, who was in charge of Latin Americn affairs for the National Security Council in 1982, said the arms shipment was "news to me."
"No one ever breathed a word of it to me," he told the Herald.
Guatemalan authorities also were surprised to hear of the arms shipment, the newspaper said.
"This is very surprising," presidential spokesman Ricardo de la Torre told the newspaper. "Generally, what we've heard is that they helped us. This is something new."

The February 1982 shipment consisted of a single planeload of rifles, ammunition, grenades, grenade launchers and radios, the Herald said. It was dropped by parachute into the jungle, where it was retrieved by the Revolutionary Organisation of People in Arms (ORPA), one of three leftist guerrilla groups fighting the Guatemalan army.

The shipment was part of the CIA's attempt to recruit Eden Pastora, a military hero of Nicaragua's Sandinista revolution, who had broken with his former colleagues. Pastora was an adviser to ORPA and demanded the arms shipment as a sign of good faith from Duane Clarridge, then head of the CIA Central American Task Force, the Herald said.
The Herald said Pastora confirmed the arms were sent.

"I don't know if Clarridge got them from the CIA or where, but he got them," the Herald quoted Pastora as saying. "We thought they came from the Cosa Nostra. The ORPA guerrillas were in an offensive then, and they really needed them."
Clarridge, who now works for General Dynamics in San Diego, would not discuss the shipment, the paper said.
After delivery of the weapons, Pastora joined the contras, but his army ultimately dissolved in 1986 and he retired to Costa Rica.
